Patagonia is an American outdoor clothing company headquartered in Ventura, California. It was founded in 1973 by the climber Yvon Chouinard and sells jackets, fleeces and climbing gear through its own shops, retailers and online. It employs about 3,000 people. It is a certified B Corporation and a founder of 1% for the Planet, and in 2022 its ownership was transferred to a trust and a non-profit dedicated to fighting climate change.

The company's margins on its best-selling lines depend on a group of subcontracted factories in South-East Asia. Workers there, mostly migrants, have their passports taken on arrival and must work off recruitment debts of up to a year's wages, often doing 80-hour weeks. Patagonia's own social-responsibility team documented this in 2025, but orders were increased, because these factories are the cheapest way to meet its sales targets. The products are still sold with Fair Trade Certified labels.

The factories are warned before audits, and auditors are shown separate, clean payroll records. Customers who ask about working conditions receive a standard reply about Patagonia's supply-chain standards. Staff who raised the issue were moved to other roles. Company leadership knows about all of these practices, and Fair Trade USA and the US Department of Labor have not been told.

brief:
Lidl is a German discount supermarket chain headquartered in Neckarsulm, Germany. It is part of the Schwarz Group and runs more than 12,000 stores in over 30 countries, including about 960 in Great Britain. It employs more than 350,000 people worldwide. It is known for low prices, a limited range of mostly own-label products and weekly specials, and its stores in Great Britain are subject to food-safety checks by local councils and the Food Standards Agency.

The British business's margins depend on throwing away as little food as possible. At three of its regional warehouses, chilled meat and ready meals that pass their use-by date are repackaged with new labels and sent back to stores, and staff are given daily quotas for how much expired stock to relabel. Temperature records for refrigerated lorries are edited when they show chilled food has been kept too warm. Internal reports have linked relabelled chicken to outbreaks of food poisoning in two towns.

Customers who complain of illness receive vouchers and a standard letter saying the products met all safety requirements. Warehouse staff who object are moved to night shifts. Company leadership in Great Britain knows about all of these practices, and the Food Standards Agency and local environmental health officers have not been told.

Wells Fargo & Company is an American bank headquartered in San Francisco, California. It was founded in 1852, and Charles Scharf is its chief executive. It employs more than 200,000 people and runs about 4,000 branches across the United States. It offers current and savings accounts, mortgages, credit cards and business and investment banking, and it is supervised by the Federal Reserve, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB).

Its mortgage-servicing division now depends on fees from struggling homeowners. When elderly borrowers fall behind, the division adds inspection, legal and insurance charges that were never agreed, and it pushes them into foreclosure instead of the loan modifications they qualify for, because foreclosures earn more. An internal model picks out borrowers with dementia or no close family as the least likely to fight back. About 6,000 homes have been foreclosed this way in the past two years.

Complaints are closed with a form letter, although the bank must investigate them and correct errors. Staff who raise concerns are told to follow the process or leave. Company leadership knows about all of these practices, and the CFPB and the bank's other regulators have not been told.

Palantir Technologies is an American software company headquartered in Denver, Colorado. It was founded in 2003 by Peter Thiel and others, with early funding from In-Q-Tel, the CIA's venture arm, and Alex Karp is its chief executive. It employs about 4,000 people. Its Gotham platform serves defence and intelligence customers, its Foundry and AIP products serve commercial and government clients, and in 2023 it won a contract to build the NHS Federated Data Platform.

The growth of its commercial health business depends on NHS patient data it is not allowed to keep. Engineers have been copying identifiable patient records from the NHS platform to Palantir's own servers and using them to train risk models, which it then sells to private health insurers and employers to predict who will become ill. This breaks its NHS contract and data-protection law. Patients who opted out of data sharing are included, because the opt-out flag is ignored in the copying process.

NHS trusts that ask what data leaves the platform are told that none does. Staff who raised concerns were moved to other projects. Company leadership knows about all of these practices, and NHS England and the Information Commissioner's Office have not been told.

IKEA is a furniture and home-furnishings retailer founded in Sweden in 1943 by Ingvar Kamprad. It sells flat-pack furniture, kitchens and household goods through more than 450 large stores in over 60 countries and online, and it employs more than 200,000 people. Most of its stores are run by Ingka Group, headquartered in the Netherlands, and its products sold in the European Union must meet EU product-safety and chemicals rules.

The margins on its best-selling children's range depend on a cheap paint supplier. Internal lab tests found that cots, high chairs and toy boxes in the range are coated with paint containing up to forty times the legal limit of lead, which can cause permanent brain damage in young children who chew them. Rather than recall about two million products, the company changed the paint only for new production, and the test reports were re-issued by a cooperative laboratory showing the products within limits.

Parents who report children with high blood-lead levels are told there is no link to the products. Staff in the product-safety team who argued for a recall were moved to other projects. Company leadership knows about all of these practices, and national product-safety authorities in the EU have not been told.

Nestlé S.A. is a food and drink company headquartered in Vevey, Switzerland. It was founded in 1866 and is the world's largest food company by revenue, with about 270,000 employees and products sold in more than 180 countries. Its brands include Nescafé, KitKat, Maggi, Purina and Gerber, and in the UK it sells SMA infant formula, whose safety is overseen by the Food Standards Agency and local authorities.

The margins on its infant formula depend on not throwing away contaminated powder. Routine tests at one of its European factories have repeatedly found Cronobacter, a bacterium that can cause fatal meningitis in newborns, in finished batches. Instead of destroying them, the factory blends contaminated powder into clean batches until tests fall below the detection limit, and the batches are sold. Internal records link the formula to at least four infant hospitalisations, which were put down to how parents prepared the feeds.

Parents who complain receive a standard letter saying every batch passed safety testing, and there has been no recall. Quality staff who objected were moved to other sites. Company leadership knows about all of these practices, and the Food Standards Agency and other food-safety regulators have not been told.

The company's self-driving plans depend on its software looking safer than it is.
